1079.title: Free grace for all
1079.hook: Arminius and Wesley stressed grace that goes before, freeing everyone to respond
1079.howItsDone: Methodist and other Wesleyan churches teach prevenient grace, God's grace going before every person and enabling them to respond, and their hymns and preaching often invite people to answer that grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, predestination: Reformed Christians resting in God's choosing, a hand that won't let go. Your line was held by his choosing.

"The God of my mercy shall prevent me." That's a psalm, in the King James Bible, and to a modern ear it sounds alarming. Prevent me? Stop me? But in the English of that Bible, to prevent could mean to come before, to go ahead of. The psalm is saying God's mercy will go out in front. Keep that old meaning in your pocket. John Wesley, the Methodist leader, liked to call one of his teachings preventing grace. Today it usually goes by a longer, Latin-flavored name: prevenient grace.
screen: `THE GOD OF MY MERCY SHALL PREVENT ME.`

segments.voice: Prevenient grace: grace that comes before. Yesterday the Reformed said God chooses first, and salvation rests on that choosing. Jacob Arminius, a Dutch teacher, and later John Wesley in England, agreed on the first part: grace must come first. Nobody climbs to God by their own strength; Augustine was right about that, they said. But they read the Bible's wide words widely. John's Gospel calls Christ "the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." Titus says: "the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men." And Jesus says, in John: "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me." So, they taught, God's grace goes ahead of everyone, not only some. It wakes the conscience. It loosens the bent will just enough that a person can say yes to God, or turn away. Wesley spoke of it as the first faint wish to please God, the first dawn of light. The yes still matters, but even the yes is a gift. Methodists and other Wesleyan and Holiness churches stand in this line, and so do some Pentecostals. The Reformed reply that it gives too much weight to the human choice; Wesleyans reply that love leaves room for a real answer, yes or no. Both sides quote scripture, both say grace first, and both pray. The first letter of John has a line both could sign: "We love him, because he first loved us." The disagreement is over what happens next.
screen: `WE LOVE HIM, BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Listen inward for a small nudge of good you've been stepping around, an apology, a call to an old friend, without inventing one, and let it grow clear. Then choose one small step that would answer it. If you pray, give thanks for the nudge itself; if you don't, notice that it came before you chose to listen.
Prevenient grace. Grace that goes before anyone chooses, reaching everyone and freeing them to answer. Arminius and Wesley stressed it.
Your line: grace goes before. Even the yes, in this teaching, is a gift. See you tomorrow.

1080.title: Why God became human
1080.hook: Athanasius: he became human that we might become godlike; Anselm asked why a God-man was needed
1080.howItsDone: Christians celebrate the Word made flesh at Christmas and in the creeds, which say that he came down from heaven for us and for our salvation and was made man; Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant teachers explain the why in different, overlapping ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prevenient grace: grace that goes before everyone, freeing each person to answer. Your line was grace goes before.

A student sits with his teacher, and the student will not let a question go. Why? If God is all-powerful, why not simply forgive? Why come down at all, be laid in a manger, and die? The teacher is Anselm, an archbishop, and he writes the whole conversation down as a dialogue, titled with the student's question in Latin: Cur Deus Homo. Why God became human. Long before him, a bishop named Athanasius had given his own answer, in one sentence people still quote. Two answers, one question.

Day three hundred met the event itself, in John's Gospel: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Not a visit in disguise. Flesh: hunger, tiredness, tears. Athanasius asked what that was for, and his answer, in an old English translation of his book On the Incarnation, is this: "He was made man that we might be made God." That sounds startling. He didn't mean people stop being creatures. He meant what the second letter of Peter means by "partakers of the divine nature": God came all the way into human life so that human life could be drawn all the way into God's. A doctor doesn't heal from across the street; he comes to the bed. Anselm came at the question from another side. Sin, he argued, is a debt of honor owed to God, and it's humanity that owes it. But the debt is too great for any human to pay; only God could pay it. So the one who pays must be both: human, because humans owe it, and God, because only God can. Hence a God-man. Christians have carried both answers. Orthodox teachers dwell on Athanasius: God became human to heal and raise humanity into his life. Anselm's argument shaped later Western thinking about the cross. Other answers sit alongside these, and some are coming soon. Earlier still, Irenaeus put it in a line today's carry borrows: he became what we are, so that we might become what he is.
screen: `ATHANASIUS: SO WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.`
`ANSELM: A DEBT ONLY A GOD-MAN CAN PAY.`

segments.voice: Ask the question slowly, the way Anselm's student did, why would God become human, without hurrying to an answer. Then bring it close to your own body, your hands, your tired back, the hunger that will come around lunchtime, all of which, in Christian teaching, God took on. If you pray, hold the line from John, the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us; if you don't, just keep the question company.
Why God became human. Athanasius: so that we might be made God. Anselm: because only a God-man could pay what humanity owed.
Your line: he became what we are. Hunger and tiredness included. Rest well.

1081.title: One person, two natures
1081.hook: Chalcedon: without confusion, change, division or separation
1081.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that hold the early creeds accept Chalcedon's definition of Christ as one person in two natures, while the Oriental Orthodox churches speak of one united nature; all of them confess him truly God and truly human.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why God became human: Athanasius said to draw us into God's life, Anselm said to pay what we owed. Your line was he became what we are.

A boat in a storm on the Sea of Galilee. Waves coming over the side. The disciples bailing, shouting. And in the back of the boat, Mark's Gospel says, Jesus is "asleep on a pillow." Worn out, like any man after a long day. They shake him awake. Then "he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still." And the sea goes flat. A tired man asleep on a cushion, then a voice the wind obeys. Same boat, same person. How do you say who that is, without dropping one half? Today's word: one person.

The Gospels keep doing this. On the way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, John's Gospel has two words: "Jesus wept." A few lines later the same Jesus stands at the grave and cries, "Lazarus, come forth." Grief, and then a voice that calls the dead. Christians searched for words that keep both. At the council of Chalcedon, bishops said Christ is one person in two natures, truly God and truly human. And they added four guard rails, each a without. Without confusion: the two aren't blended into some third thing. Without change: neither turns into the other. Without division, and without separation: there aren't two people in the boat, one sleeping and one commanding. It's one who. One of the council's Greek words for person was hypostasis: the who, the one acting in everything he does. So the same one weeps and calls Lazarus out; the same one sleeps and stills the sea. Not a man who was only very holy. Not God wearing a human costume. Both, not either. Not every church accepted Chalcedon's exact wording; some ancient churches of the east prefer to speak of one united nature, and they too confess him fully God and fully human. Day seven hundred eighty-three told that story. Today the point is the shape of the answer. It doesn't solve the mystery. It refuses to drop either half of it.

Rest one hand, palm up, on each knee: in the left, something true about your life that's hard; in the right, something true that's good. Don't let either cancel the other, or rush to decide which is really true; feel the two weights, and one breath going in and out between them. If you pray, hold the line from Mark, Peace, be still; if you don't, just keep both hands open.
One person. Chalcedon's answer: Christ is one person, truly God and truly human, two natures without confusion, change, division or separation.
Your line: both, not either. Two hands open, one breath between. I'll be here tomorrow.

1082.title: Victory over death
1082.hook: some early Christian writers saw the cross as Christ defeating death and evil
1082.howItsDone: In Orthodox churches the Easter hymn proclaiming Christ trampling down death by death is sung again and again through the Easter season, and the resurrection icon shows Christ raising Adam and Eve from the broken gates of death; Protestant and Catholic Christians also sing and preach this victory, especially at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one person, two natures, fully God and fully human. Your line was both, not either.

A gate lies flat on the ground, broken in two, its bolts scattered like dropped keys. A figure in white stands on the pieces, pulling an old man and an old woman up out of their graves by the wrists. That's the Anastasis, the resurrection icon of the Eastern churches. Other Easter icons show the women at the empty tomb. This one shows a rescue: the prison of the dead smashed open, and Adam and Eve, the man and woman from the garden, hauled out. Day three hundred two asked why the cross. Now, a bigger question: what did it actually do? Christians give more than one answer, and some hold several together. Today's answer is a battle, and a winner.
screen: `ADAM AND EVE PULLED BY THE WRISTS.`

segments.voice: The Latin name is Christus Victor: Christ the victor. In this picture, humanity is held hostage. Death, sin and the devil have us, and nobody breaks out from the inside. So God comes in. Hebrews says Christ shared our flesh and blood "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil." And why it matters: to set free those who "through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage." The enemy isn't only death. It's the fear of death, leaning on a whole life. Paul's letter to the Colossians uses the picture of a Roman triumph, a victory parade: Christ "having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it." The powers that seemed to win on Good Friday are paraded as the beaten side. Some early Christian writers told it almost like a trick. Death swallowed Jesus the way it swallows everyone, found it had swallowed life itself, and couldn't keep it down. Gregory of Nyssa even pictured a fishhook hidden in bait. Then Paul, in his first letter to Corinth, gets to taunt: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" You can hear it at Easter in the Orthodox hymn of Christ trampling down death by death. Churches can hold this picture alongside others. This one is simple: the cross was a fight, and the fight is over.

Think of something that has held you hostage, a fear, a habit, a grief, a voice that says you're finished, and give it a plain name. Picture it as that broken gate, flat on the ground. If you pray, name it to Christ as one thing he has defeated; if you don't, notice what it would feel like for that thing to have no last word.
Christus Victor. Latin for Christ the victor: the cross and the empty tomb as a battle won over death, sin and evil.
Your line: death is defeated. The gate of death lies broken on the ground. See you tomorrow.

1083.title: Satisfaction
1083.hook: Anselm pictured the cross as Christ restoring God's honor on our behalf
1083.howItsDone: Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's wording ask God to forgive their debts, and in some churches the language of Christ paying what humanity owed is heard in hymns, sermons and the prayers at communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christus Victor: a broken gate, and death that swallowed life and couldn't keep it down. Your line was death is defeated.

"Forgive us our debts." That's how the Lord's Prayer reads in Matthew's Gospel, in the old King James words. Not mistakes. Not trespasses. Debts. As if every wrong leaves an unpaid bill behind it. Anselm, the archbishop who asked why God became human, took that picture seriously. Some historians link his thinking to a world of lords and oaths, where honor was owed, and a broken promise had to be made good. His question was hard and clear: if sin is a debt to God, what does it take to settle it? Yesterday's picture was a battlefield. Today's is a ledger.

Forget the modern meaning, the feeling after a good meal. In Anselm's picture, satisfaction means making amends: doing what's needed to put a wrong right. He lays it out in his dialogue Why God Became Human. Every creature owes God honor: its whole life and will, turned toward God. Sin is holding that back. And here's the trap. Even if you lived perfectly from tomorrow on, you'd only be paying what you already owed for tomorrow. Nothing is left over to cover yesterday. So the debt stands. Anselm says a wrong against honor can end only two ways: it's made good, or it's punished. God, he says, chooses to make it good. Not a penalty, but a repair. On day one thousand eighty we heard who Anselm thought could do that: only one who is both God and human. Christ's freely given life, which he never owed to death, is a gift so great it more than covers what humanity held back. Paul has his own picture of a bill wiped out: "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... nailing it to his cross." Not every church tells the story with Anselm's ledger, and those who do build on it in different ways. Notice what it is not. In Anselm's telling, the cross isn't punishment. It's payment. That difference comes back tomorrow.

Think of a debt someone paid for you; it doesn't have to be money: someone covered for you, made good on a promise you broke, stayed up so you could sleep. Notice the size of it, and that you couldn't have paid it yourself. If you pray, hold that picture next to the cross and say thank you; if you don't, just stay with the person who paid.
Satisfaction. In Anselm's picture, making amends for a wrong against God's honor: a debt humans owe and only the God-man can pay.
Your line: he paid what we owed. A gift bigger than the bill. Go gently.

1084.title: Substitution
1084.hook: the Reformers stressed Christ bearing the penalty in our place (Isaiah 53:5)
1084.howItsDone: In Reformed, Lutheran and evangelical churches, sermons, hymns and communion prayers speak of Christ dying in the believer's place, and some churches read Isaiah 53 during Holy Week.

segments.voice: Yesterday, satisfaction: Anselm's ledger, a debt we owe and can't pay. Your line was he paid what we owed.

A prison door swings open in Jerusalem, and a man named Barabbas walks out into the daylight. Mark calls him a man held with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. He was in chains. Then the Roman governor lets him go: Pilate "released Barabbas unto them, and delivered Jesus, when he had scourged him, to be crucified." One man walks free. Another goes to the cross. The Gospels never say what Barabbas did next, or whether he ever stood near Golgotha and looked up. But some readers have stood in his sandals ever since.

Substitution means one in the place of another. Christians reading the cross this way go back to a song in Isaiah about a servant who suffers: "But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." Notice the little words: for our, upon him. The wounds belong to one, the healing to others. The first letter of Peter picks up the song: Christ "his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree." Here's what's new since yesterday. Anselm said a wrong is made good or punished, and put the cross on the payment side. The Reformers, Luther and Calvin among them, stressed the other side: the penalty for sin was real, and Christ bore it, in our place. Paul says it sharply to the Corinthians: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him." Luther called this a happy exchange: Christ takes what is ours and gives us what is his. Some who hold this picture call it their peace: the verdict has already been carried. Other Christians hold it more lightly, or worry it can sound like a Father punishing an unwilling Son. Those who hold it close answer that Father and Son act as one, out of the same love: God himself carries the cost. Churches weigh it differently. At its heart is Barabbas, and the open door.

Picture the door open in front of you, daylight outside, and name one thing you carry that you can't put down by yourself: a wrong you did, a weight you can't fix. If you pray, thank God for bearing what you couldn't; if you don't, notice what it would be like to walk through that door with your hands empty.
Substitution. One in the place of another: Christ bearing the penalty of sin so that others go free.
Your line: in my place. The door is open, and Barabbas walks out. That's today, done.

1085.title: Love's example
1085.hook: Abelard stressed the cross as love so great it changes us
1085.howItsDone: Some Christians meditate on the cross as a sign of God's love, for example in Good Friday services, hymns about the cross, and the Stations of the Cross, letting what they see shape how they treat others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, substitution: Barabbas walking free while another went to the cross. Your line was in my place.

A Roman officer is on duty at an execution. The Gospels don't say what he expected. But this death goes differently. Luke says that from the cross Jesus prays for the people killing him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." When it's over, the officer, a centurion, says something nobody ordered him to say. Luke records it: "Certainly this was a righteous man." Nothing was paid to him. No argument convinced him. He watched how someone loved, all the way to the end, and Luke says he glorified God.

Moral influence is the name later writers gave to a picture stressed by Peter Abelard, a teacher in medieval Paris. The last few days asked what the cross does to death, to a debt, to a penalty. Abelard asked what it does to us. His answer, in a commentary on Paul's letter to the Romans: the cross is God's love shown so plainly that it wins our love in return, and that love sets us free. He leaned on a verse from that letter: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Commendeth means shows, puts on display. Not after we cleaned up. While we were yet sinners. Love goes first, and in this picture, love answers. Jesus said, in John's Gospel, "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Here the cross is that greater love, and seeing it changes the one who sees. People argued with Abelard in his own day. Bernard of Clairvaux worried this made the cross only an example, a beautiful one, but no rescue. Some readers of Abelard point out that he spoke of more than example: he called this love a real power that frees. Churches can keep this note inside their other pictures: whatever else the cross does, it shows love. The centurion's line is this picture in one sentence: he watched, and he spoke.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE CROSS DO TO US?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who reliably sets you off, and picture the moment it usually happens. Before the usual reaction, picture being loved first, while you were still at your worst, and let one small different response come: a pause, a softer word, a question instead of a verdict. If you pray, you can ask for that love.
Moral influence. The picture of the cross as love shown so plainly that it wins our love and changes us, stressed by Abelard.
Your line: love that changes us. In this picture, love goes first, and love answers. Until tomorrow.
